newsitem.title: CHINA: China anti-speculation measures most serious yet.
newsitem.headline: China anti-speculation measures most serious yet.

text.p: China's latest ban on state bank funds flowing into shares is the government's most serious move yet to try to stop speculation and cool the overheated stock markets, local and foreign brokers said on Friday.
Domestic currency A shares on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock markets are expected to fall sharply over the next week as state banks unwind their positions and other investors flee, they said.
Foreign currency B shares will also move lower in the short term, but the falls will not be as drastic as the more liquid domestic A market, brokers said.
Both the Shenzhen and Shanghai markets plunged in early Friday trading, as investors took stock of new measures aimed at cooling speculation and driving state banks off the bourses.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, issued an urgent directive after the markets closed on Thursday banning state banks from trading on the stock market and giving them 10 days to unwind their positions.
The central bank also barred state banks from trading treasury debt repurchase agreements (repo), a major source of funds for stock trading, from Friday.

"This is pretty serious," said Bruce Richardson, chief Shanghai representative for HG Asia Ltd. "On the face of it the government is basically saying the main sources of funds (to the stock market) will be cut off."
"State banks have been major traders on the state debt repo market, which has served as a fund reservoir for the stock markets," said a local trader.
"The ban could possibly lead to a loss of up to half the A share market's liquidity," he said.
China in May introduced measures to cool the stock markets, including a huge 30 billion yuan new share quota for 1997.
Although the new ban on state bank funds restates existing rules, brokers said the markets were still too buoyant.
"We will continue to see further downward adjustments in the near future," said Zhang Jun, a researcher with China's Guotai Securities. "I think the effects will be felt into next week."
Shanghai A shares lost 5.5 percent on Friday morning, while the B index lost 2.62 percent.
The Shanghai A share market could fall to around 1,100 points, from Friday morning's close of 1,343.246, Zhang said.
But B shares will not be affected as much because that market attracts less speculative money and the government does not want to scare off foreign investors, analysts said.
Brokers put support for Shanghai's B index at around 80 points.

"The B shares will definitely weather this because the market is for foreigners and the government wants to maintain the feel-good factor," said Alex Conroy, of ING Barings in Shanghai. "They're trying to make market stability the key point."
The Shenzhen market is also expected to stay at low levels in the short term in choppy trading due to the announcment and rumours of yet more market-cooling measures to come.
Shenzhen's A share index fell 5.92 percent in the Friday morning session, to end at 444.54 points. The B index lost 3.86 percent, to close the morning session at 150.72 points.
But brokers said the Shenzhen markets will recover as the return of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 nears.
